title: Soil erosion

definition.text: The wearing away of the upper layer of soil, a form of soil degradation.

facts.text: It is driven by erosive agents: water, ice, snow, wind, plants such as uprooted trees, and animals including humans.
Following those agents, it is divided into water, glacial, snow, wind (aeolian), zoogenic and human-caused erosion such as tillage erosion.
It can go on slowly and almost unnoticed, or so fast that it causes a serious loss of topsoil.
Human activities have raised the rate of erosion worldwide by about 28 times the natural rate.
On-site, accelerated erosion lowers farm productivity and can collapse ecosystems by stripping nutrient-rich upper layers, sometimes ending in desertification.
Off-site, it silts waterways, feeds eutrophication of water bodies and damages roads and houses with sediment.
Water and wind erosion together account for about 84% of the world's degraded land.
About 75 billion tons of soil are eroded from the land each year; one global model puts the loss to water alone at almost 36 billion tons.

conflicts.text: Human activities have increased the rate of soil erosion globally by 10–40 times.
conflicts.note: Erosion page gives a 10–40 times range where Soil erosion gives about 28 times.

conflicts.text: About 75 billion tons a year is eroded, about 13–40 times as fast as the natural rate.
conflicts.note: Same quantity (human-accelerated versus natural rate) given as 13–40 times.

notes: The 75 billion t figure covers all erosion; the 36 billion t figure (S:e770d11817ca) is water erosion only, so they are not a conflict.

title: Erosion

definition.text: The removal of soil, rock or dissolved material from one place on the Earth's surface by processes such as flowing water or wind, and its transport to another place where it is deposited.

facts.text: Erosion differs from weathering, which involves no movement of material.
Removing material as clastic sediment is physical or mechanical erosion; removing it by dissolution is chemical erosion.
Eroded sediment or solutes may travel only a few millimetres or for thousands of kilometres.
Agents include rainfall, river flow, waves, glaciers, flooding, wind, groundwater and mass movements such as landslides and debris flows.
Physical erosion is usually fastest on steep slopes, and its rate also responds to rainfall, storminess, wind speed, wave fetch and temperature.
Transport of eroded material ends in deposition, when it arrives and settles at a new location.
Where erosion outpaces soil formation it destroys the soil; slower erosion can still prevent soil features that need time to develop.
Inceptisols form on eroded landscapes that, if stable, would have developed into Alfisols.

notes: Lead says human activity raised soil erosion 10–40 times (S:bd6212f48748); see the conflict note on Soil erosion.

definition.text: The removal of soil by rainfall and by the surface runoff it produces.

facts.text: Runoff begins when the soil is saturated or when rain falls faster than water can infiltrate.
Runoff with enough flow energy carries loosened soil particles down the slope as sediment.
Rain and runoff cause four main types of erosion, in rising severity: splash, sheet, rill and gully erosion.
Concentrated runoff cuts small channels called rills; if runoff keeps deepening them, they may grow into gullies.
Water erosion removes soil mainly from the middle and lower parts of a slope rather than from hilltops.
A global model estimates that almost 36 billion tons of soil are lost to water every year.

definition.text: Erosion caused when falling raindrops strike bare soil and knock particles loose.

facts.text: A falling raindrop makes a small crater in the soil and throws out soil particles, which then move off with surface runoff.
It is usually seen as the first and least severe stage of water erosion, followed by sheet, rill and gully erosion.
On level ground without wind, ejected particles can travel up to 0.6 m vertically and 1.5 m horizontally.
Larger, faster raindrops carry more kinetic energy and throw particles further; plant cover and crop residues soften the impact.

definition.text: The even erosion of soil or other material across a wide area by a thin, unchannelled layer of flowing water.

facts.text: It works in two steps: rainsplash loosens small particles, then a thin, uniform sheet flow carries them a short distance.
Each event moves material only a short way, but frequent repetition makes up for the small change per episode.
It is common on freshly ploughed fields and bare, unconsolidated ground; one rainstorm can remove up to a hundred tons of fine particles per acre.
On an uneven hillslope, sheet erosion may give way to erosion in small channels called rills, which can merge into gullies.

definition.text: Erosion by water flowing continuously along a linear channel, which deepens valleys and wears away river banks.

facts.text: Stream erosion cuts both downward, deepening the valley, and headward into the hillside, creating head cuts and steep banks.
Early on, erosion is mostly vertical and makes V-shaped valleys; once a base level is reached it turns lateral, widening the floor into a floodplain.
Most stream erosion happens during floods, and pebbles and boulders carried by the water also abrade the bed, a process called traction.
Bank erosion wears away a river's banks, as distinct from scour of its bed; heavier runoff from built-up land sharply increases it.

definition.text: The wearing away of shorelines, mainly by currents and waves, with changes in sea level also playing a part.

facts.text: Waves erode by hydraulic action, pounding, abrasion (corrasion), corrosion of rock such as limestone by carbonic acid, and attrition of the carried load.
Abrasion, in which waves hurl their sediment load at cliffs, is the most effective and rapid form of shoreline erosion.
Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast; erosion occurs where less sediment arrives from upcurrent than is carried away.
Sea-level rise caused by climate change has greatly increased coastal erosion rates.

definition.text: The loss of material from a landscape in dissolved form, as solutes.

facts.text: It contrasts with physical erosion, which removes rock or soil as solid particles of sediment.
It is usually calculated from the dissolved load carried by streams.
Sinkholes and other karst features are an extreme example of chemical erosion.
Anders Rapp pioneered its study in work on Kärkevagge published in 1960.

definition.text: Erosion by moving glacier ice, mainly through abrasion, plucking and ice thrusting.

facts.text: In abrasion, debris frozen in the base of the ice scrapes, polishes and gouges the bed like sandpaper on wood; in plucking, the glacier breaks off pieces of bedrock.
In ice thrusting, a glacier frozen to its bed carries large sheets of frozen sediment forward as it surges.
Glaciers carve U-shaped valleys, a steady shape estimated to take about 100,000 years to form.
Glacial erosion and meltwater leave landforms such as moraines, drumlins, ground moraine (till), kames and glacial erratics.

title: Wind erosion

definition.text: Erosion by wind, which lifts and carries away loose particles (deflation) and wears down surfaces with windborne grains (abrasion).

facts.text: It is a major landscape-shaping force, especially in arid and semi-arid regions.
It drives land degradation, desertification, harmful airborne dust and crop damage, above all where deforestation, urbanization and farming have raised it above natural rates.
Deflation moves particles by surface creep (rolling or sliding), saltation (short bouncing hops) and suspension (fine particles lifted and carried far).
Saltation does most of the work (50–70%), followed by suspension (30–40%) and surface creep (5–25%).
Silty soils such as loess are the most affected, because silt particles detach and travel easily.
It needs strong winds and is worst in drought; on the Great Plains, wind erosion losses can be up to 6100 times greater in drought years than wet years.
Tillage worsens it by drying and breaking up the soil, and clearing trees from fields gives the wind long, open runs.
Vegetation shelters soil from the wind, and windbreaks of trees and shrubs along field edges significantly reduce wind erosion.

related: Wind Erosion on European Light Soils

definition.text: The power of rainfall to cause soil erosion, set mainly by how much rain falls and how intensely.

facts.text: The amount and intensity of precipitation is the main climatic control on water erosion, especially when the soil surface lacks plant cover.
Larger, faster raindrops have more kinetic energy and displace soil particles further than small, slow ones.
In places such as the Midwestern United States and the Amazon, rainfall intensity is the main determinant of erosivity.
In western Europe, erosion follows low-intensity stratiform rain on already saturated soil, so total rainfall matters more than intensity.
Rainfall erosivity is the R factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation.
The Global Rainfall Erosivity Database (GloREDa) covers 3,625 stations in 63 countries and was used to map erosivity worldwide at about 1 km resolution.

definition.text: The protection that living plants and the litter they leave give the soil against wind and water erosion.

facts.text: Vegetation makes the soil more permeable to rain, which reduces runoff, and shelters it from the wind.
Plant roots bind the soil and interweave into a solid mass that resists both water and wind erosion.
Removing vegetation increases the rate of surface erosion.
In forests, the litter and humus of the forest floor absorb raindrop impact and let water percolate slowly; the floor, more than the canopy, prevents surface erosion.
Raindrops regain terminal velocity within about 8 metres, so drops falling from a tall canopy can still strike the ground at full speed.
Increasing vegetative cover is the most effective known way to prevent both wind and water erosion.

definition.text: The influence of a slope's steepness and length on how fast runoff flows and how much soil it erodes.

facts.text: Topography sets the speed of surface runoff, and that speed sets how erosive the runoff is.
Longer, steeper slopes, especially poorly vegetated ones, erode much faster in heavy rain than short, gentle ones.
Steep terrain is also more prone to mudslides, landslides and other gravity-driven erosion.
The Universal Soil Loss Equation represents slope length and steepness with its L and S factors.

definition.text: The acceleration of soil erosion by farming practices that loosen, bare or compact the soil.

facts.text: Unsustainable farming raises erosion one to two orders of magnitude above the natural rate, far beyond what soil formation can replace.
Tillage, which breaks soil into finer particles, is a primary cause; mechanized deep ploughing makes far more soil available for water to carry off.
Monocropping, farming steep slopes, row crops, surface irrigation, and pesticides and fertilizers that kill soil-binding organisms also raise erosion.
Heavy grazing strips plant cover and severely compacts soil, both of which increase erosion.
Erosion is size-selective: the finer eroded fraction loses more total phosphorus than the soil as a whole.
At farm sites in the Appalachian Mountains, intensive practices have caused erosion up to 100 times the natural regional rate.
Growing potatoes carries a higher erosion risk than growing cereals or oilseed crops.
Over a third of the U.S. Corn Belt has lost its topsoil entirely; switching to no-till would cut erosion from U.S. fields by more than 70 percent.

title: Deforestation and soil erosion

definition.text: The rise in soil erosion that follows removal of forest cover and its protective forest floor.

facts.text: Deforestation exposes mineral soil by removing litter and humus, removes the roots that bind soil, and compacts it under logging machinery.
After fire or logging, erosion stays low as long as the forest floor remains intact, but severe fires followed by heavy rain cause much more erosion.
Slash-and-burn clearing of tropical forest is one of the largest contributors to erosive soil loss worldwide.
In Brazilian studies, runoff and soil loss fell to forest-like levels after 4–5 years of regrowth, and a 15-year fallow restored the original soil.

contested_note: Sources call it a debate whether slash-and-burn with forest regrowth or permanent pasture and cash crops after logging does more lasting damage to tropical soils.

definition.text: The increase in erosion and polluted runoff caused by construction, roads and paved urban land.

facts.text: Construction strips vegetation, alters drainage and compacts soil; asphalt and concrete then increase surface runoff and surface wind speeds.
Sediment in runoff from urban areas, especially roads, is often heavily contaminated with fuel, oil and other chemicals.
The extra runoff changes how much water flows through nearby watersheds and how fast, fills them with polluted sediment and greatly increases bank erosion.

title: Climate change and soil erosion

definition.text: The expected rise in soil erosion as warming brings heavier rainfall and alters vegetation, litter, soil moisture and frozen ground.

facts.text: Warmer temperatures are expected to intensify the water cycle, with more extreme rainfall and so more erosion unless measures are taken.
Studies by Pruski and Nearing suggest about a 1.7% change in soil erosion for each 1% change in total precipitation.
Early 21st-century studies predicted rainfall erosivity rising by 17% in the United States, 18% in Europe and 30 to 66% globally.
Other routes include shifts in plant canopy and litter, loss of soil organic matter, winter snow turning to erosive rain and thawing permafrost.

related: Effects of climate change on agriculture

definition.text: The harm done to rivers, lakes, coasts and their life by excess sediment washed in from eroding soil.

facts.text: Soil erosion, especially from farmland, is considered the leading global cause of diffuse water pollution.
Sediments are pollutants in their own right and also carry attached pesticides and heavy metals; eroded soil also carries fertilizers into rivers, causing eutrophication.
Silt smothers fish spawning beds by filling gaps between gravel, cuts food supply and clogs gills; plant, algal and invertebrate diversity declines.
The Yellow River carries over 1.6 billion tons of sediment to the ocean each year, mostly from water erosion on the Loess Plateau.
On Madagascar's central plateau, gullies called lavakas may supply 84% of river sediment, turning rivers dark red-brown and killing fish.
Watershed development near coral reefs is a primary cause of sediment stress, as sediment smothers and abrades corals and feeds algal blooms.
Removing an estimated 135 million m3 of sediment from water erosion likely costs over 2.3 billion euros a year in the EU and UK.

definition.text: The unconfined flow of water over the ground surface, as opposed to flow in stream channels; also called overland flow.

facts.text: It forms when rain, stormwater or meltwater cannot soak in fast enough, because the soil is saturated or rain arrives faster than the soil absorbs it.
Impervious areas such as roofs and pavement are a common cause, since water cannot soak into the ground there.
It is a major part of the water cycle and the primary agent of soil erosion by water.
The land area whose runoff drains to a common point is called a drainage basin.
Soil storage absorbs light showers; on ancient Australian and southern African soils, dense proteoid root networks can prevent runoff even in heavy rain.
Runoff carries soil particles about 0.001 to 1.0 mm across; larger ones settle quickly, while small ones stay suspended over long distances.
It is a nonpoint source of pollution, carrying petroleum, pesticides and fertilizers; agricultural runoff drives nutrient pollution and eutrophication downstream.
In towns it is a primary cause of urban flooding, from street flooding to damp and mould in basements.

definition.text: Runoff that forms when rain falls faster than the ground can absorb it and surface hollows are already full.

facts.text: It is also called Hortonian overland flow, after Robert E. Horton, or unsaturated overland flow.
It is commonest in arid and semi-arid regions with intense rain and sealed soil surfaces, and in towns where pavement blocks infiltration.
It differs from saturation-excess flow, which begins only once the soil itself is saturated.

definition.text: Runoff produced at once when rain keeps falling on soil that is already saturated and whose surface hollows are full.

facts.text: It is also called saturated overland flow or Dunne runoff.
Moisture left from earlier rain (antecedent soil moisture) sets how soon soil saturates: the wetter it starts, the sooner runoff begins.
Saturated soils absorb less rain, so a given volume of rainfall produces more runoff and more erosion.

definition.text: Water that soaks into a hillside upslope, flows sideways through the soil and seeps back out near a channel; also called throughflow.

facts.text: On its way, runoff shrinks as some water evapotranspires, some is held in small surface hollows and some infiltrates.
The water that remains ends up in a river, lake, estuary or ocean.

definition.text: Surface runoff from rain, landscape irrigation and car washing created by urbanization.

facts.text: Roads, parking lots, sidewalks and roofs carry polluted stormwater to storm drains instead of letting it percolate through soil.
Less water reaches groundwater, so the water table falls and droughts worsen, while more water left on the surface causes flooding.
Most municipal storm sewer systems discharge the stormwater untreated into streams, rivers and bays, where erosion and siltation can be major problems.

definition.text: Measures that limit the harm done by surface runoff: land-use controls, erosion controls, flood control and controls on chemical use.

facts.text: Land-use codes encourage narrow sidewalks and pavers set in earth to let as much water as possible infiltrate in towns.
Since the 1960s some governments have required builders to use erosion and sediment controls such as straw bales, silt fences and limits on bare graded ground.
Flood control uses holding ponds (detention basins) to buffer peak flows and energy dissipators to slow channel flow.
Chemical controls include double containment of underground tanks, fewer allowed pesticides and stricter rules for fertilizers and herbicides.

definition.text: Erosion in rills, shallow channels no more than a few centimetres deep cut into soil by flowing surface water.

facts.text: Smaller incised channels are microrills and larger ones are gullies.
Hillslope runoff cuts rills into unprotected soil, as on farmland left bare, after deforestation or during construction.
Rills are easy to see when first cut, so they are often the first sign of an erosion problem.
Flow in rills is typically a few centimetres deep or less, so its hydraulics differ greatly from flow in streams and rivers.
Rill flow may carry nearly ten times as much as interrill areas, and in moderate rain can move rock fragments up to 9 cm across.
Tractors compact soil so water runs over it, and wheel tracks channel that water into rills.
Without soil conservation, rills can grow into gullies or, in semi-arid regions, badlands; under good management contour tilling repairs them.

definition.text: The start of a rill, when the shear stress of runoff exceeds the soil's shear strength and water begins to tear particles loose.

facts.text: Sandy and loamy soils are especially prone to rills, while dense clays resist them.
Slope steepness mainly controls rill formation and depth; slope length and soil permeability set how many rills form.
Each soil has a threshold slope below which rills cannot form; on many non-cohesive slopes it is about 2 degrees, at a shear velocity of 3 to 3.5 cm/s.
Up to 37% of erosion in rilled areas may come from collapse of rill sidewalls undercut and weakened by water.

definition.text: Erosion that cuts gullies, steep-sided channels formed in soil by running water, mass movement or both, usually on hillsides or in floodplains.

facts.text: Gullies are metres to tens of metres deep and wide, have a distinct headscarp and lengthen by headward erosion at a knickpoint.
They carry intermittent flow after intense or long rain or snowmelt, and often begin where a rill has been neglected and kept growing.
Hillslope cultivation, clearing, overgrazing and tracks worn by livestock or vehicles start or speed up gullying.
Processes include incision and bank erosion by flow, collapse of gully walls, groundwater seepage and collapse of soil pipes in dispersive soils.
Gullies cut farm productivity and supply sediment that chokes downstream waters; losses are greatest in unstable, dispersive soils.
The Universal Soil Loss Equation cannot simulate gullies, though they can supply 10–80% of total erosion on cultivated and grazed land.
On Madagascar's high central plateau, gully furrows commonly exceed 50 metres deep and 1 kilometre wide.

definition.text: Altering water flow through a gully to reduce scouring, let sediment build up and allow plants to return.

facts.text: Good land management prevents gullies: vegetation along drainage lines, evenly spread runoff, high soil organic matter and no over-cultivation.
Drop structures, pipe structures, grass chutes and rock chutes carry water safely down to the gully floor.
Sediment settling on flatter stretches lets vegetation re-establish, and damaged areas should be fenced off until restoration is complete.
Evidence on how well gully controls work is scattered, and terrain, climate and landscape can make them fail.

definition.text: The erosion, transport and deposition of sediment by wind at or near the Earth's surface.

facts.text: Wind is most effective where vegetation is sparse, soil moisture is lacking and loose sediment is plentiful.
Worldwide, water erodes more than wind, but wind erosion is important in arid and semi-arid regions such as deserts.
Aeolian deposits also occur outside dry climates, along shorelines and on glacial outwash; much of North America and Europe is underlain by Pleistocene windblown sand and loess.
Wind sorts sand from silt and clay, so it builds separate sandy deposits (ergs) and silty ones (loess), with loess laid down further from the source.
Collisions between windborne grains (attrition) round and frost sand grains and are a major source of dust 2–5 microns across.
Wind carries minerals from the Sahara to the Amazon basin, and Saharan dust has formed red clay soils in southern Europe.
The name comes from Aeolus, the Greek god who kept the winds.

definition.text: The lifting and removal of loose surface material by turbulent wind.

facts.text: It works through surface creep, saltation and suspension, with saltation likely accounting for 50–70% of it.
Most deflation zones are floored by desert pavement, a sheet of rock fragments left behind once fines are removed, which shields the material below.
Deflation hollows called blowouts range from dimples 0.3 m deep to Mongolian hollows 8 km across and 60 to 100 m deep.

definition.text: The wearing of rock and landforms by wind-driven grains, also called corrasion.

facts.text: Once thought a major cause of desert erosion, it was judged much less important by the mid-20th century; features like mushroom rocks are now credited to other processes.
Wind usually lifts sand only a short way: most stays within 50 cm of the surface and practically none rises above 2 m.
Yardangs, rock ridges up to tens of metres high streamlined by desert winds, are widely attributed to abrasion and form mostly in soft material such as silt.
Polished or faceted stones called ventifacts are rare, needing abundant sand, strong winds and no vegetation.

definition.text: The movement of sediment by wind through suspension, saltation (skipping) and creep (rolling or sliding).

facts.text: Grains start moving at the fluid threshold wind speed; impacts then keep transport going until wind falls below the lower impact threshold, a hysteresis.
Turbulence holds fine particles in suspension, letting wind separate grains under 0.05 mm from coarser ones and carry them far.
Saltation matters most for grains up to 2 mm; landing grains launch others and push heavier ones forward as creep, up to 25% of grain movement in deserts.
Vegetation suppresses aeolian transport: a plant cover of as little as 15% stops most sand movement.

definition.text: A mound or ridge of sediment heaped up by the wind, independent of any obstacle.

facts.text: Dunes have a gentle windward slope and a steep downwind avalanche slope called the slipface.
Transverse dunes such as crescent-shaped barchans form under one prevailing wind; linear dunes run for tens of kilometres; star dunes have more than two slipfaces.
Vegetated parabolic dunes are crescents whose ends point upwind, formed where plant patches meet active sand such as blowouts.
Ralph Bagnold named the barchan and the linear seif dune; John Tilton Hack added vegetation-shaped parabolic dunes in 1941.

title: Dust storm

definition.text: A storm in which strong wind blows loose sand and dirt off dry ground, common in arid and semi-arid regions; also called a sandstorm.

facts.text: By one definition, it is a wind storm carrying enough dust to cut visibility below 1 kilometre.
Saltating sand grains strike the ground and break off finer dust, which then travels in suspension.
Drought, wind, wildfire and poor farming and grazing cause them; intensive tillage in dryland farming and bare ground without crops or cover crops are especially risky.
Gusts come from thunderstorm outflows or from dry cold fronts, the type common in the Dust Bowl years.
They remove soil from drylands, preferentially taking organic matter and the light, nutrient-rich particles, and their abrasion damages young crops.
Saharan dust storms have increased about 10-fold since the 1950s, causing topsoil loss in Niger, Chad, northern Nigeria and Burkina Faso.
Inhaled dust can cause dust pneumonia, and prolonged exposure can cause silicosis.
Deposited dust can help: rainforests of Central and South America gain mineral nutrients from the Sahara, and ancient dust deposits form fertile loess.

notes: Event: China began its great green wall tree planting in the Gobi in 1978 (S:e3a31c8b64a4); sandstorm frequency fell 20% in 2009–2014 (S:d0fc53f85253).

definition.text: Fine particles of solid matter; on Earth, mostly particles in the air from soil lifted by wind, volcanic eruptions and pollution.

facts.text: Dust that stays suspended in the atmosphere for a long time is considered an aerosol.
Windborne dust comes mainly from saltation in dry regions, where strong winds strip mostly silt-sized material up to 1/16 mm across.
Grazing, ploughing, vehicles and other human activity further destabilize dust source areas.
Dust-producing surfaces cover about one-third of the global land area, roughly 13 billion hectares.
Saharan dust reaches the Caribbean and the Amazon basin, about 132 million tons crossing the Atlantic each year, and can affect temperatures and rainfall.
Soil dust from wind erosion is a major source of air pollution and often carries toxic chemicals such as pesticides or petroleum fuels.
Dust from erosion suppresses rainfall, and dust events have been linked to declining coral reef health in the Caribbean and Florida since the 1970s.
Dust poses a health risk to children, older people and people with respiratory diseases.

definition.text: The suppression of airborne solid particles smaller than 500 micrometres.

facts.text: Environmental agencies such as the US EPA require facilities that generate fugitive dust to minimize it; new urban housing developments are the most frequent violators.
Construction and demolition sites are sprayed with water, and dust is kept from being tracked onto nearby roads.
Unpaved lots and dirt roads are paved or gravelled, or stabilized with water, vegetable oil, calcium chloride or other suppressants.
Benefits include fewer allergic reactions, pneumonia and asthma attacks, and better visibility and road safety.

title: Wind Erosion on European Light Soils
article: Wind Erosion on European Light Soils

definition.text: An EU-funded research project (WEELS) that built a field-scale wind erosion model from test sites in Lower Saxony, Scania and Suffolk.

facts.text: It ran from 1997 to 2000 as a collaboration of University College London, the Geological Survey of Lower Saxony, Lund University and Wageningen University.

notes: Frame seed, but a single research project; the brief says local projects are not course entries.

definition.text: Soil erosion in cultivated fields caused by the movement of soil during tillage.

facts.text: Growing evidence shows it is a major erosion process on farmland, surpassing water and wind erosion in many fields, especially on sloping and hilly land.
The pale, eroded hilltops often blamed on water erosion are actually caused by tillage erosion, which strips organic-rich topsoil from convex spots.
Its rate depends on tillage erosivity, set by the implement's design, speed and depth, and on landscape erodibility, set by slope shape and soil properties.
It arises from changes in tillage translocation (soil moved by tillage) across a field, which grows with slope gradient and curvature.
Soil is lost from hilltops and field-boundary downslopes and piles up in hollows and against boundaries, building tillage banks and terraces.
As topsoil thins, tillage mixes poorer subsoil into the plough layer and spreads it across the field, cutting crop productivity for a long time.
Soil degraded by tillage erosion likely becomes more erodible by water and wind.
It is reduced by lighter tillage (fewer, slower, shallower passes, smaller implements), contour tillage, ploughing furrows upslope and moving soil back to eroded hilltops.

definition.text: Ways of quantifying tillage erosion, either by tracking soil moved by tillage or by measuring where soil is lost and gained.

facts.text: Translocation is measured by mixing point or bulk tracers into plots and comparing their positions before and after tillage.
Soil loss and gain show up as changes in surface elevation, compared against an uneroded fence line or hedgerow or surveyed with RTK GPS or photogrammetry.
Changes in soil organic matter can also indicate loss, but many other factors affect it, so the method is unreliable.
Since the 1980s, radioisotopes such as Cs-137 and Pb-210 have given much more accurate soil erosion estimates.

definition.text: Computer models that simulate how tillage moves soil along a hillslope or across a field.

facts.text: One-dimensional hillslope models such as TEP and TillERI use slope length, gradient and the erosivity of the tillage operation to give erosion rates and risk.
WaTEM calculates both water and tillage erosion on a digital elevation model, treating tillage redistribution as diffusion in the steepest-slope direction.
Field-scale models such as SORET and TillEM add the direction of tillage, moving soil both parallel and perpendicular to it.

definition.text: A widely used empirical model (USLE) that estimates long-term average annual soil loss from water erosion as the product of six factors.

facts.text: It multiplies rainfall erosivity (R), soil erodibility (K), slope length and steepness (L and S), cover and management (C) and support practices (P).
It was built in the U.S. from erosion plot and rainfall simulator experiments, using data the USDA Soil Conservation Service collected from the 1930s.
The unit plot standard has LS = 1 (a 9% slope 22.1 m long), bare fallow, up-and-down-slope tillage and no conservation practice.
K can be read from a nomograph using particle size, organic matter, structure and permeability, and LS from a slope chart; C and P must come from plot data.
It is the most commonly used soil loss model and the main one used by U.S. agencies, and helped implement the multibillion-dollar U.S. conservation program.
Though plot-based, it is often applied to watersheds, continents and the globe, and it cannot simulate gully erosion.
Revised (RUSLE) and Modified (MUSLE) versions remain in use, and newer models such as G2 still build on it.

title: Support practice factor
article: Universal Soil Loss Equation#Description of USLE

definition.text: The P factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation, a soil loss ratio expressing how much conservation practices reduce erosion.

facts.text: It is hard to determine because regional maps of conservation practices are usually lacking, so it is often estimated from land use and slope.
Field boundaries such as stone walls, hedgerows, earth banks and lynchets effectively prevented or reduced erosion in pre-industrial farming.
A European P-factor model was built from a survey recording stone walls and grass margins, and landscape archaeology mapping can fill gaps in the data.

definition.text: Using data and models to predict where, and how fast, erosion may happen in the future.

facts.text: There are dozens of models; some treat long-term natural erosion within landscape evolution, while many quantify human-accelerated soil erosion.
Most predict average annual soil loss from a plot, field or catchment under different land management.
Most consider only water erosion; few predict wind erosion, and models of tillage or gully erosion are rare.
Process-based models solve equations for detachment, transport and deposition, while empirical models relate soil loss statistically to environmental and management factors.
No model is fully process-based yet; research favours process-based models, but the empirical USLE remains the standard for conservation planning.
Two widely used North American models are the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) and the Water Erosion Prediction Project model (WEPP).
Predicted and observed erosion rates often differ widely, so models remain better research tools than regulatory instruments unless calibrated locally.
Erosion models are non-linear, which makes it hard or impossible to scale predictions from small plots up to large areas.

definition.text: Potential erosion from all sources except gullies divided by the soil's T value, the erosion rate above which long-term productivity may suffer; also called the erodibility index.

facts.text: It is used for U.S. conservation compliance and the Conservation Reserve Program, which requires land to have an index above 8.
In the United States, farmers cultivating highly erodible land often must follow a conservation plan to qualify for agricultural assistance.

definition.text: The inherent lack of resistance of a soil or rock to erosion.

facts.text: A highly erodible material loses more material for the same amount of work done by erosive processes.
Soil erodibility is a lumped value for how a soil profile responds each year to detachment and transport by raindrops and surface flow.
In the Universal Soil Loss Equation it is the K factor, estimated from silt and very fine sand content, clay content, organic matter, structure and permeability.
Clay-rich soils resist erosion better than sandy or silty ones because clay binds particles together.
Organic matter makes soil more resistant by coagulating colloids into a stronger, more stable structure; long cultivation depletes it and raises erodibility.
Wet or compacted soils absorb less rain, so more water runs off and erodes.
Stone cover protects against erosion, which matters greatly in Mediterranean countries.
For channels and dams, erodibility in a shear stress model can be measured with a hole erosion test or a jet erosion test.

definition.text: Solid material made of loose particles that is carried to a new place and deposited there.

facts.text: It is produced by weathering and erosion and moved by wind, water, ice or gravity.
Water (fluvial processes) moves it most often: beach sands and river deposits are fluvial, dunes and loess are windblown, and moraines and till are carried by ice.
Buried sand and silt can be lithified into sedimentary rocks such as sandstone and siltstone.
Sediment is classified by grain size, shape and composition; size is measured on the log base 2 phi scale, from colloid to boulder.
Because clay names both a size range and a group of minerals, the term is ambiguous for sediment.
Seas and lakes accumulate terrigenous sediment from land, mostly supplied by rivers, along with sediment formed in the water, often from organisms.
Lake bed sediments that have not yet hardened into rock record past climates.

definition.text: The description of sediment particles by three parameters: overall form (sphericity), roundness of corners and surface texture.

facts.text: Form is spherical, platy or rodlike, measured from the lengths of a grain's long, intermediate and short axes using formulas such as Krumbein's or Sneed and Folk's.
Roundness runs from very angular to very rounded and is usually judged against comparison charts rather than calculated.
Surface pits, fractures and scratches, studied mostly on quartz grains with an electron microscope, reveal a grain's transport history.
Frosted grains are particularly characteristic of windblown sediment.

definition.text: The movement of solid particles, from clay to boulders, by gravity together with the water, air or ice in which they are carried.

facts.text: Its study is mostly used to predict whether erosion or deposition will happen, how much, and over what time and distance.
Stronger flows raise lift and drag on a particle, while larger or denser particles tend to fall out of the flow.
Water moves larger particles than air because it is denser and more viscous; rivers usually carry sand and gravel, and big floods move cobbles and boulders.
Fluvial transport shapes ripples, dunes, floodplains and river patterns, and moves sediment by eroding and depositing on the bed.
Wind moves fine sediment, building dune fields and soils from airborne dust; glaciers carry a wide range of sizes and deposit them in moraines.
Changes in flow power cause erosion or deposition, locally behind boulders and inside meanders, and regionally after dam building or removal or base level change.
On hillslopes, soil creep, tree throw, burrowing animals and landslides move regolith downslope; as slopes near the angle of repose, erosion rates rise steeply.
When human activity raises the suspended load enough to fill channels, the problem is called siltation.

title: Sediment delivery ratio
article: Sediment#Erosion and agricultural sediment delivery to rivers

definition.text: The fraction of gross erosion on a catchment (interrill, rill, gully and stream erosion) expected to reach the river outlet.

facts.text: Sediment transfer and deposition can be modelled with sediment distribution models such as WaTEM/SEDEM.
WaTEM/SEDEM estimates put the sediment delivery ratio in Europe at about 15%.
Sediment reaching river basins brings management and siltation costs.

title: Erosion control

definition.text: The practice of preventing or controlling wind and water erosion in farming, land development, coastal areas, river banks and construction.

facts.text: Effective controls manage surface runoff and help prevent water pollution, soil loss, habitat loss and property damage.
Many controls are physical barriers of vegetation or rock that absorb some of the energy of the wind or water.
Methods include crop rotation, conservation tillage, contour ploughing, cover crops, hydroseeding, riparian buffers, strip farming and windbreaks.
Terracing is an extremely effective control, practised around the world for thousands of years.
Mixed cropping and crop rotation reduce erosion, crop residues soften raindrop impact under conservation tillage, and forages' fibrous roots anchor the topsoil.
Agroforestry, mixing crops with trees, is efficient against erosion, especially in rainy tropical climates and on severely degraded land.
On construction sites, erosion controls are combined with sediment controls such as sediment basins and silt fences; in towns they are part of stormwater programmes.
Bank erosion is natural, but where people want to hold a river in place, they line its banks with riprap or gabions.

notes: Event sentence: mathematical models of soil erosion since the 1920s and 1930s, including an early paper by Albert Einstein applying Baer's law (S:473fe89f3948).

definition.text: A practice or device that keeps eroded soil on a construction site so it does not wash off and pollute nearby waters.

facts.text: Sediment controls are usually paired with erosion controls, which prevent erosion in the first place and so reduce the need for them.
They are mostly temporary, though some also serve for stormwater management.
Common controls include silt fences, sediment basins and traps, fiber rolls, straw bale and sand bag barriers, storm drain inlet protection and turbidity curtains.
All U.S. states require erosion and sediment controls on construction sites above a set size; federal rules apply from 1 acre (0.40 ha).
Controls must be installed before land clearing and grading begin and maintained through the whole disturbance phase.
Montgomery County, Maryland, began the first local government sediment control program in 1965, followed by a Maryland statewide program in 1970.

definition.text: Systems that clear sediment-laden construction runoff by adding flocculants and then filtering or settling the water.

facts.text: Active systems pump the water and dose it with natural polymers, synthetic polymers or inorganic flocculants to cut total suspended solids before discharge.
Cationic flocculants such as chitosan can cause hypoxia in fish, so anionic flocculants are best practice in open systems.
Passive systems use gravity flow through ditches with self-dosing gel flocculants, jute filters and sedimentation ponds, needing no power and little skill.
Stormwater management facilities are usually designed with Stokes' law to remove particles larger than 40 microns.

definition.text: The movement of rock or soil down slopes under the force of gravity; also called mass movement.

facts.text: Unlike other erosion, the moving debris is not carried along in a medium such as water, wind or ice.
Types include creep, solifluction, rockfalls, debris flows and landslides, acting over seconds to hundreds of years.
Water usually aids it without being a transporting medium; with more water, landslides grade into debris avalanches, earthflows, mudflows and finally sheetfloods.
Movements are broadly creeps or landslides, and subsidence is sometimes counted as a form of mass wasting.
It is often the first stage in moving weathered material in mountains, carrying it down to where streams and glaciers can pick it up.
Weak, unconsolidated material, steep slopes, freeze-thaw or heavy rain, and undercutting by excavation or erosion all promote it.
Slow creep deforms roads and breaks pipelines, while rapid landslides can be deadly.
It is mitigated by slope stabilization, walls, catchment dams for rockfall and debris flows, afforestation and better drainage of source areas.

definition.text: The deposits and landforms left by mass wasting, usually subtle but occasionally spectacular.

facts.text: Soil creep shows itself in curved tree trunks and tilted fences and poles, and freeze-thaw creep builds small steps called terracettes.
Solifluction leaves lobed or sheet-like deposits whose rock fragments point perpendicular to the deposit's contours.
Rockfall builds talus slopes at the foot of cliffs, and landslides leave scarps and step-like terraces.
Debris flows leave long, narrow tracks of very poorly sorted material, often with levees, and build much of the upper slopes of alluvial fans.

definition.text: The slow downward movement of soil and rock on a gentle slope; also called soil creep.

facts.text: Creep looks continuous but is the sum of many tiny, separate movements driven by gravity; the steeper the slope, the faster the creep.
Friction holds slope material in place; as a slope steepens, the part of gravity pressing into it shrinks, so friction falls.
A little water gives soil cohesion, like damp sand in a sandcastle, but saturation fills the pores and creates a slip plane.
Clay that swells when wet pushes soil downhill and settles at the new position as it dries; freeze-thaw and heating-cooling cycles move soil the same way.
Objects ride along: old churchyard headstones lean and sit metres from where they were set, and trees grow curved and fences tilt.
Plant roots bind loose material and draw off excess water, though they add weight; bare slopes are more likely to move.
Creep deforms roads and breaks pipelines, so engineers drive pilings deep enough to keep it from undermining foundations.
Modelled as diffusion of regolith, linear on gentle slopes and non-linear on steep ones, creep rounds ridges over long timescales.

definition.text: Gradual downslope mass movement of soil linked to freezing and thawing.

facts.text: Johan Gunnar Andersson coined the term in 1906 for water-saturated debris moving in periglacial regions; such slow movements were later tied to freeze-thaw instead.
It is typical of arctic and alpine climates, where soil thawed and saturated in summer creeps down moderate, sparsely vegetated slopes over permafrost.
It is slow but widespread across mountains and periglacial lowlands, and because it needs cold, humid conditions it is used to infer past climates.
It builds tongue-shaped lobes and sheets; its deposits are poorly stratified diamicton, sometimes with buried organic soils.

definition.text: Any of several forms of mass wasting with relatively rapid ground movement, such as rockfalls, mudflows, slope failures and debris flows.

facts.text: Landslides happen on steep and gentle slopes alike, from mountains to coastal cliffs and under water.
Gravity drives them: a slope fails when the shear strength of its material falls, the shear stress on it rises, or both.
Many are set off by a specific event such as heavy rain, an earthquake or a road cut, though the trigger is not always identifiable.
Natural causes include wetting and rising pore water pressure, loss of vegetation and soil structure after wildfire, undercutting by rivers or waves, weathering and earthquake shaking.
Deforestation, cultivation, construction, earthworks and removing deep-rooted plants that bind colluvium to bedrock all aggravate them.
Land degradation weakens the hold of vegetation on soil and, with extreme rainfall, makes erosion and landslides more frequent.
Saturated slope material can become a debris flow or mudflow that carries off trees, houses and cars and blocks rivers.
Landslides under water or into water can generate tsunamis.

definition.text: A scheme sorting landslides into six types of movement (fall, topple, slide, spread, flow and slope deformation), each found in both rock and soil.

facts.text: David Varnes proposed a tighter classification in 1978; it was revised by Cruden and Varnes in 1996 and most recently by Hungr, Leroueil and Picarelli in 2014.
Falls are blocks in free fall, topples rotate away from a vertical face, and slides move as an intact body over planar or spoon-shaped (rotational) shear surfaces.
Spreads crack and extend sideways, flows move fluidised dry or wet material, and slope deformations are slow, distributed movements.
Soil classes include clay and silt rotational slides, sensitive clay spreads, debris flows, mud flows, earthflows and soil creep.
Moving material is called rock, earth or debris; earth has less than 20% by weight of particles over 2 mm, debris more.
Narrower definitions restrict landslides to slumps and translational slides that do not involve fluidisation, excluding falls, topples, lateral spreads and mass flows.
Typical slope angles are 45–90 degrees for falls and topples, 20–45 degrees for translational slides and 20–40 degrees for rotational slides.
Classifying a landslide by its activity and movement velocity matters most for judging future hazard.

definition.text: Landslides grouped by the depth of their sliding surface: within the soil mantle or weathered bedrock (shallow), or well below tree rooting depth (deep-seated).

facts.text: Shallow slides reach from a few decimetres to some metres deep; debris slides and debris flows are usually shallow.
They often occur where permeable soil lies over less permeable soil, which traps water, builds pressure and lets the saturated topsoil slide.
Deep-seated slides involve deep regolith, weathered rock or bedrock, often move along faults or bedding planes, and show concave head scarps and steep toes.
Deep-seated landslides shape landscapes over geological time and supply sediment that strongly alters stream courses.

title: Mudflow

definition.text: A fast-moving flow of debris and soil that has been liquefied by added water; also called a mudslide.

facts.text: Mudflows move at three to five metres per second; their clay makes them more fluid than debris flows, so they travel farther over gentler slopes.
They contain at least 50% silt- and clay-sized material and up to 30% water.
Many begin as slides triggered by heavy rain, snowmelt or groundwater and turn into flows as they take up water.
Whether mud starts to flow depends on its grain size, water content and the slope.

definition.text: Analysing the factors behind past landslides to map where future ones are likely, to reduce losses and guide land-use planning.

facts.text: Factors used are usually grouped into geomorphology, geology, land use and land cover, and hydrogeology.
Geographic information systems handle the many layered factors, and before-and-after aerial photos and satellite images record landslide distribution and triggers.
Prediction assumes that future landslides will occur under the same conditions as past ones.
Hazard maps should show past events and clearly mark probable locations of future ones.

definition.text: Tracking slope movement to judge danger, issue timely alerts and plan protective measures.

facts.text: Remote sensing uses InSAR for precise, large-scale displacement, repeated LiDAR point clouds, optical satellite imagery and drones.
Ground-based methods include GPS, topographic surveys of marked targets and ground-based radar.
Geotechnical instruments include piezometers for pore water pressure, borehole inclinometers, extensometers across cracks and tiltmeters.

definition.text: The effects of changing temperature, rainfall and evapotranspiration on where, how often and how strongly landslides occur.

facts.text: The effects vary strongly between areas, can raise or lower landslide activity, and must be studied regionally.
Warming can reduce landslides where higher evapotranspiration dries soils and growth of vegetation is stimulated.
It increases them through faster snowmelt and rain on snow, permafrost thaw that removes the cohesion of interstitial ice at high elevation, and glacier retreat.
More extreme rainfall focuses infiltration and increases runoff events that may trigger debris flows.

definition.text: The ability of a soil or rock slope to withstand movement; the opposite condition is slope instability or slope failure.

facts.text: It is studied in soil mechanics, geotechnical engineering and engineering geology, to explain failures and to prevent, slow or stop slope movement.
Stability is set by the ratio of available shear strength to acting shear stress, expressed as a safety factor along a potential sliding surface.
A slope is globally stable if the safety factor exceeds 1 along every potential sliding surface from top to toe; the smallest value represents the whole slope.
Safety factors between about 1 and 1.3 mark marginally stable slopes that need monitoring or stabilization.
Triggers include intense rain, snowmelt, saturation, earthquakes, internal erosion (piping), toe erosion, loading by buildings and cutting for roads.
After heavy rain, pore water pressure on the slip surface reduces effective normal stress and friction, while the added groundwater increases soil weight.
Failures in pure clay are often close to circular, while slab-shaped slips strip a layer of soil off the underlying bedrock.
Some moisture can steady a slope, but saturation acts as a lubricant; fine clay and silt soils hold more water than sandy ones.

definition.text: Engineering work on slopes that raises their stability and lessens the effect of landslides.

facts.text: Methods are classed as geometric (reshaping the slope), hydrogeological (lowering groundwater or drying the material) and chemical or mechanical (raising shear strength, anchors, nails, piles).
Vegetation is a widely used bioengineering method where landslides are shallow: roots reinforce the upper soil, and interception and transpiration dry it.
Slopes are also stabilized by flattening, piles or retaining walls, grouting, and consolidation by surcharging or electro-osmosis.
Installing drainage paths significantly improves stability by reducing destabilizing forces.

definition.text: Static or dynamic, analytical or empirical methods for evaluating the stability of natural slopes and of dams, embankments and excavations in soil and rock.

facts.text: It is used to design safe embankments, road cuts, open-pit mines, excavations and landfills.
It needs site data on soil and rock properties, slope geometry, groundwater and discontinuities; water pressure in pores and fractures lowers material strength.
Limit equilibrium is the most common and simplest method, but complex failures such as progressive creep or liquefaction need numerical modelling.
Simple 2-D circular analysis is widely used, but finding the most probable slip plane is a primary difficulty, and real failures in mixed soils are not always circular.

definition.text: The two-way link between slopes and the plants growing on them, which can either strengthen or weaken a slope.

facts.text: The relationship depends on the soil type, the rainfall regime, the plant species, the slope aspect and the steepness of the slope.
Plants act on slopes in four main ways: wind throw, removal of water, the added mass of the vegetation (surcharge) and mechanical reinforcement by roots.
Wind throw topples a tree and exposes its root plate and the soil beneath; it matters for a single tree, less for a stand, where inner trees are sheltered.
Plant mass matters only where large trees grow: a tree 30–50m tall may load a slope with roughly 100–150 kN/m2.
Large trees at the toe of a slope prone to rotational failure could raise its factor of safety by 10%; planted at the top they could lower it by 10%.
Felling large trees at a slope's toe removes both their drying effect and their load, and in clay soils the resulting suction can draw in water and soften the soil.
Judging how plants alter a slope rests on knowing its underlying stability as a function of soil type, age, horizon development and compaction.

title: Transpiration and slope stability
article: Vegetation and slope stability#Removal of water

definition.text: The stabilising of slopes by plants that draw water out of the soil and transpire it, lowering soil pore water pressure.

facts.text: Lower pore water pressure offsets the strength a soil loses on wetting; the effect shows as drier soil around trees.
Plants transpire little in wet weather, so the strength gain fades when storms saturate a slope, though transpiration still makes failure after heavy rain less likely.
Studies in Malaysia linked high root length density to low soil water content, higher shear strength, lower permeability and fewer slope failures.
Plants can deepen desiccation cracks in dry weather, letting water reach a slip plane, but shading by their foliage limits the drying and cracking.

title: Root reinforcement of soil
article: Vegetation and slope stability#Mechanical reinforcement of roots

definition.text: The strengthening of soil by roots that grow across potential failure planes, act as piles and limit surface erosion.

facts.text: Roots crossing a potential failure plane raise shear strength by binding particles and anchor unstable surface soil to deeper stable layers or bedrock.
In the root reinforcement model, a root stretched across a slip plane develops a tensile force that passes to the soil through cohesion and friction.
Root strength generally extends only to about 1 m (3.3 ft), while most slope failures occur at 1.2–1.5 m (3.9–4.9 ft) depth.
Fine roots of shrubs and grasses hold the surface soil against sheet wash and overland flow, with a cohesion likened to geosynthetic mesh, mostly in the top 1 m.

title: Root pull-out resistance
article: Vegetation and slope stability#Tensile root strength contribution and pull out resistance

definition.text: The force a root resists before being pulled out of the ground, usually only a little less than its laboratory tensile strength.

facts.text: Laboratory tests on many species and root diameters put tensile root strength at about 5–60 MN/m2.
Unbranched roots fail in tension and slip out with little resistance; branched roots hold a high force that declines as branches fail, or break in stepped stages.
Thicker roots resist pull-out more than thinner ones, and roots tend to fail at weak points such as branching points, nodes or damage.
A root strengthens a slope only with enough embedment and adhesion in the soil; for engineering, in situ pull-out tests measure its contribution.

definition.text: A highly sensitive glaciomarine clay, also called Leda or Champlain Sea clay, that can change from a solid into a watery fluid when disturbed.

facts.text: Once remolded, quick clay keeps far less strength than it had on first loading, because its clay particle structure is highly unstable.
It consists of very fine silt and clay-sized particles from glacial grinding, first laid down in the sea.
It is found only in lands near the North Pole glaciated in the Pleistocene: Russia, Canada, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Alaska.
In Canada it is tied mainly to the Pleistocene Champlain Sea, in the Ottawa Valley, the St. Lawrence Valley and the Saguenay River region.
Sudden liquefaction, set off by earthquake vibrations or massive rainfall, causes its landslides; in Canada alone it is linked to more than 250 mapped landslides.
Liquefaction usually affects sandy or non-plastic silty soils; quick clay is one of the rare cases in clay.
It is a particular challenge for civil engineering, and known deposits are now commonly tested before any major development.

definition.text: The sequence by which glacial rock flour, laid down loosely in the sea and later raised above it, became a weak and water-rich clay.

facts.text: At the height of the last glaciation, about 20,000 years ago, ice pressed the land down and the sea, reaching far inland, received the ground-up rock.
Loose settling of silt and clay in seawater gave an unusual flocculation: a strongly bonded soil skeleton glued by mobile sea-salt ions.
Post-glacial rebound then lifted the clay above the sea, and soft rainwater and snowmelt weakened its ionic glue, leaving a loose skeleton holding much water.
A normal topsoil cover absorbs ordinary stresses, but a large earthquake, extra load near a slope or saturating rain can disturb the clay and start liquefaction.

title: Electrical double layer

definition.text: The cloud of balancing cations that surrounds every negatively charged clay platelet, whose thickness depends on the salinity of the water.

facts.text: Clay particles carry permanent and pH-dependent negative charges, balanced by cations such as Na+ held on their surfaces, in interlayers or in pore water.
In salty water the double layer is compressed, so the platelets flocculate into stable aggregates; adding salt to a suspension likewise thins the layer.
When rain leaches salt out of uplifted marine clay, the layer expands and stronger repulsion disperses the platelets (peptization), destabilising the clay.
Adding salt back compresses the layer again, and quick clay rapidly regains its strength.

notes: No page of its own; the double layer is also described on Alkali soil (S:c859277ee535), Colloid (S:63c3e5fee19d) and Electrokinetic remediation (S:029dfd19a9f5). A charge or colloids chapter may prefer to own it.

title: Quick clay landslides

definition.text: Landslides in quick clay, which are retrogressive: they usually start at water and work their way upslope.

facts.text: They usually advance at slow walking speed, but deep quick clay on slopes can collapse much faster or slide in large chunks, and slides have reached kilometres inland.
Because topsoil hides the clay, vulnerable sites are usually found only by soil testing, so settlements and roads were often built on them.
A slide at Verdal, Norway, in 1893 killed 116 people; at Rissa in 1978 about 33 hectares of farmland liquefied and flowed into a lake within a few hours.
Engineering precautions include lightweight polystyrene fill, vertical wick drains and groundwater cutoff walls that keep water out of the clay.

notes: Individual slides (Verdal, Saint-Jean-Vianney, Rissa, Gjerdrum and others) appear only as examples; none is drafted as its own entry.

title: Dust Bowl

definition.text: A decade of severe dust storms and drought, 1930–1940, that badly damaged the farming and ecology of the High Plains and North American prairies.

facts.text: It hit hardest in western Kansas, the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, southeast Colorado and northeast New Mexico; its drought and erosion affected 100 million acres (400,000 km2).
It combined natural causes, above all severe drought, with human ones: settlers destroyed the topsoil by not using dryland farming methods that prevent wind erosion.
Deep plowing of the virgin prairie had removed the native deep-rooted grasses that held soil and moisture through droughts and high winds.
Cotton farmers left fields bare in winter, when High Plains winds are strongest, and burned the stubble, stripping the soil of organic matter and surface cover.
Drought came in three waves, 1934, 1936 and 1939–1940; it dried the topsoil to a powder, and failed crops left plowed fields open to the wind.
Black blizzards of dust reached the East Coast; a two-day storm in May 1934 dropped 12 million pounds (5,400 tonnes) of dust on Chicago.
In many regions more than 75% of the topsoil had blown away by the end of the 1930s.
A key result was the government's greatly expanded role in land management and soil conservation.

title: Dust Bowl government response

definition.text: The US federal programmes of the 1930s that answered the Dust Bowl with soil conservation, tree planting and farm relief.

facts.text: The Soil Erosion Service was set up in August 1933 under Hugh Hammond Bennett; moved to the Department of Agriculture in 1935, it became the Soil Conservation Service, now the NRCS.
The Civilian Conservation Corps planted the Great Plains Shelterbelt, over 200 million trees from Canada to Abilene, Texas, to break the wind and hold soil and water.
Farmers were taught crop rotation, strip farming, contour plowing and terracing, and from 1937 were paid a dollar an acre to adopt soil-conserving methods.
By 1938 the conservation effort had cut the amount of blowing soil by 65%.
