title: Economic legacy of the Dust Bowl

definition.text: The lasting fall in farmland value and population that followed the Dust Bowl's loss of topsoil.

facts.text: By 1940, relative to low-erosion counties, farmland value per acre had fallen 28% in high-erosion counties and 17% in medium-erosion counties.
In highly eroded areas less than 25% of the original agricultural losses were ever recovered.
Thinner topsoil favoured a shift from wheat to livestock and hay, but farmers were slow to switch, partly because bank failures cut off credit.
The economy adjusted mainly through population decline in the more eroded counties, both in the 1930s and through the 1950s.

definition.text: A very fine powder formed by the erosion of clay-limestone terrain, found mostly in deserts.

facts.text: It forms a surface horizon of pulverised, weakly cohesive soil protected under a thin crust.
It derives from ancient lake muds or certain argillaceous rocks and is one of the desert surfaces that produce dust.
Invisible from the surface, it can collapse under a vehicle and trap it in a quicksand-like mass; it makes part of Egypt's Qattara Depression impassable to most vehicles.

title: Water cycle

definition.text: The continuous movement of water, changing form as it goes, between reservoirs on, above and below the Earth's surface.

facts.text: Its fluxes are evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, sublimation, infiltration, surface runoff and subsurface flow, all powered by energy from the sun.
Rain reaching land either flows over the ground as surface runoff or soaks in by infiltration, becoming soil moisture or groundwater.
Shallow infiltrated water may seep back to streams or be taken up and transpired by plants; deeper water recharges aquifers, where it can stay for thousands of years.
Evapotranspiration combines water transpired by plants with water evaporated from the soil.
About 505,000 km3 (121,000 cu mi) of water falls as precipitation each year, 398,000 km3 (95,000 cu mi) of it over the oceans.
Flowing water reshapes the land through weathering, erosion and deposition, and runoff carries almost all eroded sediment and phosphorus from land to water bodies.
A global study of stable water isotopes found that not all soil moisture is equally available for groundwater recharge or plant transpiration.

distinct_from: Land use and the water cycle

title: Land use and the water cycle
article: Water cycle#Land cover and land use changes

definition.text: The local and regional changes to the water cycle that follow changes in land use and land cover.

facts.text: Urbanization, farm expansion and deforestation can increase soil compaction and impervious cover, lowering soil infiltration capacity and raising surface runoff.
Locally, deforestation reduces soil moisture, evaporation, rainfall and snowfall.
Stormwater drains lower runoff rates and raise groundwater recharge, while leaking sewers add recharge but can contaminate groundwater.

definition.text: Water that comes from precipitation, including heavy rain and meltwater from hail and snow.

facts.text: It may infiltrate and become groundwater, pond in depressions, evaporate or run off; most runoff reaches streams and other water bodies untreated.
In forests the soil absorbs much stormwater, and plants reduce it further by improving infiltration, intercepting rain and taking up water through their roots.
Impervious surfaces and compacted soil let less rain infiltrate, so more runoff forms, raising stream discharge and causing erosion and flooding.
Because the water is flushed away during storms, little of it recharges groundwater or feeds stream baseflow in dry weather.
Runoff carries trash, sediment, nutrients, bacteria, pesticides, metals and petroleum byproducts; the first flush of a storm is usually the most concentrated.
Phosphorus dissolved from fertilizers or bound to sediment from construction and farm runoff feeds algae and toxic cyanobacteria blooms in lakes.
Treatment facilities are usually designed with Stokes' law to settle particles larger than 40 micron and to hold water back against downstream flooding.

definition.text: The control of both the quantity and the quality of stormwater.

facts.text: Its best management practices include engineered devices such as retention ponds and routine practices such as street sweeping.
Technical aims include controlling flooding and erosion and building retention basins, filter vaults and vortex separators that remove coarse solids.
Nature-based options such as ponds, swales and constructed wetlands work alongside pipes and concrete channels and can also give habitat.
Passive treatment uses gravity flow through ditches and pipes, with gel flocculants, jute fibre filters and silt retention mats to settle sediment.

definition.text: Sinkhole collapses caused when urban stormwater drains down through karst ground and carries soil and rock fragments away.

facts.text: In undisturbed karst, soil and rock fragments choke the openings and limit their growth, and the drainage stays balanced with most storms.
Urban karst areas lack surface streams, so extra runoff from roofs and streets moves down through the ground; once flow can move soil and rock, openings grow fast.
Under a roof of competent limestone there is often no surface warning before an opening collapses, so planners are advised to avoid karst for new development.

definition.text: The downward vertical movement of the Earth's surface, caused by natural processes or by human activity.

facts.text: It involves little or no horizontal movement, which sets it apart from slope movements.
Causes include groundwater dissolving carbonate rock, gradual compaction of sediments, mining, pumping of groundwater or petroleum, and tectonic warping of the crust.
Pumping of groundwater or petroleum has lowered the ground by as much as 9 meters (30 ft) in many places, at costs of hundreds of millions of US dollars.
In karst, a weakened cave roof can collapse and drop rock and earth into the void, forming sinkholes that may be many hundreds of meters deep.
The weight of high buildings can press down the soil beneath them, a problem already felt in New York City, the San Francisco Bay Area and Lagos.
Lowered ground raises flood risk, especially on river flood plains and deltas, and uneven settlement can tilt or crack buildings.

definition.text: The sinking of the ground as clay-rich soils dry and shrink with the seasons, and its rise again when they rewet.

facts.text: Clay's very small particles make clay-rich soils sensitive to changes in moisture content.
Foundations above the depth reached by seasonal drying move with the soil, which can crack buildings with tapering cracks.
Growing trees dry the soil cumulatively; when a tree declines or is felled the soil heaves, rising and spreading for up to 25 years as the deficit reverses.

title: Runoff

definition.text: The flow of water across the land, a major part of the water cycle.

facts.text: Water flowing over land before it reaches a watercourse is surface runoff or overland flow; once in a watercourse it is streamflow, or channel runoff.
Surface runoff forms when water cannot infiltrate fast enough, because the soil is saturated, rain arrives faster than it can be absorbed, or surfaces are impervious.
Channel flow comes from hillslope runoff, groundwater flowing out of the ground and pipe discharges; it is measured with stream gauges or estimated by the Manning equation.
Floods occur when the volume of water exceeds a channel's capacity; a record of flow over time is called a hydrograph.

notes: Overlaps the Surface runoff seed (chunk 02); kept as the broader term covering channel runoff. Fold into Surface runoff at the merge if judged redundant.

definition.text: A model of how rainfall on a drainage basin is converted into runoff.

facts.text: It turns a rainfall event, entered as a hyetograph, into a surface runoff hydrograph, and must be calibrated before use.
The linear reservoir model is well known but of limited use; a non-linear reservoir applies more widely, but only where rain falls roughly evenly over the catchment.
Large study areas are split into sub-catchments whose hydrographs are combined by flood routing.

definition.text: An empirical number, CN, used in hydrology to predict direct runoff or infiltration from rainfall excess.

facts.text: It was developed by the USDA Soil Conservation Service, now the Natural Resources Conservation Service, from runoff measured on small catchments and hillslope plots.
A curve number depends on the area's hydrologic soil group, land use, treatment and hydrologic condition.
CN ranges from 30 to 100: lower numbers mean more permeable soil and low runoff potential, higher numbers more runoff.
No runoff starts until the initial abstraction, such as infiltration and interception, is met; it was long taken as 0.2 S, but 0.05 S may suit urban watersheds better.
The method works storm by storm and should not be applied to a single annual rainfall total.
Curve numbers are adjusted for antecedent moisture: dry (AMC I), average (AMC II) and moist (AMC III).
It is widely used as an efficient way to estimate approximate direct runoff from a rainfall event.

definition.text: The dry stalks of cereal plants left after the grain and chaff have been removed, an agricultural byproduct.

facts.text: It makes up about half the yield by weight of cereal crops such as barley, oats, rice, rye and wheat.

Straw bales are sometimes used to control sediment on construction sites, but they often protect water quality poorly and need much upkeep, so the US EPA prefers silt fences, fiber rolls or geotextiles.
It is also spread as ground cover after wildfires, used in in-stream check dams, and makes an excellent mulch.
Mixed with clay-rich subsoil and water it binds earth building materials such as cob and adobe.

definition.text: An artificial pond with a permanent pool of water and vegetation around its edge, built to manage stormwater runoff.

facts.text: It differs from a detention basin, or dry pond, which holds water only for a while, and from an infiltration basin, which sends stormwater to groundwater through permeable soils.
Impervious urban surfaces rush rain into drains; the pond contains the surge and releases it slowly, reducing flooding downstream.
It also traps suspended sediment, often abundant in stormwater from construction and road sanding, while its plants take up soluble nutrients.
It can stand in for the natural absorption of a forest lost to development, and serves for erosion control and groundwater recharge.

definition.text: The alteration of a landscape, for example turning natural land over to farming or housing, or dividing it into building lots.

facts.text: Conversion to building land brings road building, topsoil abrasion, soil compaction, chemical change from soil stabilization, impervious surfaces and polluted runoff.
Construction seals much of the soil off from rainfall and the nutrient cycle, so the soil under buildings and roads is in effect consumed and made infertile.
New farmland usually comes from forest, savanna or grassland cleared by assarting or slash-and-burn; reclaiming wasteland or sealed ground is rarer for lack of fertile soil.
Economic land improvement can mean ecological degradation, such as salinization from saline irrigation water, or erosion and desertification after drainage.

definition.text: A channel built to gather and carry stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution from it.

facts.text: It is a vegetated, mulched or xeriscaped drainage course with gently sloping sides of less than 6%, built on soil with no more than 5% clay.
It is designed to keep water in the swale as long as safely possible: plants catch and settle pollutants, which then decompose or are broken down by soil bacteria.
It slows runoff, recharges groundwater and reduces flooding and erosion, and suits places with much impervious surface that must handle a storm's first flush.
In permaculture, swales are used to harvest water.

definition.text: A temporary fabric fence used on construction sites to keep sediment carried by stormwater runoff out of nearby waters.

facts.text: Geotextile fabric is stretched between stakes along a contour, its lower edge buried in the soil, so that runoff pools behind it and sediment settles out.
Fine particles soon clog the fabric; no sediment-retention device filters stormwater for long.
It is widely used for its low cost and simple design, but field tests show generally poor results, often from bad placement, installation or maintenance.
Static slicing, which pushes the fabric into a slot cut by a blade and then compacts the soil, has proved the most effective installation method since 1998.

definition.text: A geotechnical laboratory test of a soil's resistance to erosion, used above all for internal erosion in embankment dams.

facts.text: A small hole, typically 6 mm, is drilled through a soil sample compacted in a mould, and water forced through it erodes and widens the hole while the flow is measured.
Plotting erosion rate against hydraulic shear stress gives the critical shear stress at which a leak starts to erode, and the erodibility that sets how fast erosion then proceeds.
A modified version adds a pitot-static tube to measure total head; it gives much smaller critical shear stresses, closer to other tests such as the jet erosion test.

title: Jet erosion test

definition.text: A geotechnical test, done in the field or the laboratory, that measures a soil's resistance to erosion with a jet of water.

facts.text: A turbulent jet strikes the soil at constant hydraulic head; where its shear stress exceeds the soil's critical value it scours a hole, whose depth is measured over time.
Fitting the erosion rate gives erodibility and critical shear stress, used in designing vegetated channels, road embankments, dams, levees and spillways.
Its jet erosion index, which correlates with erodibility, typically ranges from 0 to 0.03.
As of 2017 no method for soil erodibility was universally accepted, and depending on the fitting method, erodibility for a given critical stress can vary up to 100 times.

contested_note: The test's underlying assumptions have been criticised, and other erosion tests can give inconsistent erodibility values.

definition.text: The sudden mass wasting of a stream bank, when gravity on its rock and soil exceeds the cohesive and adhesive forces holding them together.

facts.text: All streams erode their banks by friction, shearing and solution; floods, helicoidal flow on the outside of bends and downcutting rills and gullies speed this up.
Extra weight near the edge, soil saturation from rain, irrigation or septic systems, groundwater undermining and loss of deep-rooted vegetation can all set off failure.
The toe zone, between ordinary and low water level, is most exposed to erosion; most banks are layered, with cohesionless soils interbedded with cohesive ones.
Failure may be hydraulic, geotechnical, tectonic or gravitational; cohesive soils fail on rotational or planar surfaces, non-cohesive soils by avalanching.

definition.text: The structural and vegetative measures used to keep river banks from eroding and failing.

facts.text: Common options are lime stabilization, retaining walls, riprap, sheet piling, deep vegetation, windrows and trenches, sacks and blocks, gabions, soil-cement, and keeping structures back from the bank.
Riprap, rock laid to resist erosion, is expensive and can fail but covers large areas; gabions, stone-filled wire boxes, suit steep banks where flow is too fast for riprap.
Trees add deep, dense roots; shrubs and fascines of willow or cottonwood cuttings staked in trenches root and hold the soil, the most labour-intensive but cheapest method.
On steep banks trees may fail to stabilise the toe, and their own weight can bring the bank down.

definition.text: A temporary tube of straw, coconut fibre or similar material laid on construction slopes to control erosion and trap sediment.

facts.text: Rolls are laid along contours in shallow trenches 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 cm) deep and staked down, with more rows on steeper slopes and one at the slope's base.
They slow surface runoff without channelling it, letting water through while sediment stays uphill; properly installed, they trap sediment better than straw bales.
They should not be used on very steep land prone to mudslides, landslides or creep, and rolls that are poorly staked can be carried off by high flows.

definition.text: A temporary pond on a construction site that captures soil washed off in rain storms and protects the water quality of nearby waters.

facts.text: Sediment-laden runoff settles in the pond before the water is discharged.
Basins suit construction sites of 5 acres (20,000 m2) or more; smaller sites use sediment traps, small embankments along low ground or above storm drain inlets.
After earthmoving ends, a basin may be cleaned out and kept as a permanent detention or retention basin for stormwater.

title: Internal erosion

definition.text: The formation of voids inside a soil as seeping water removes material.

facts.text: It happens when seepage through the pores and cracks of a dam or its foundation exerts enough hydraulic force to detach particles and carry them out.
It causes about half of embankment dam failures and is the second most common cause of levee failure.
It may show little outward sign, often only a sand boil that can be hidden under water, and a dam may breach within hours of the evidence becoming obvious.
Piping is its progressive growth, eroding back from the downstream exit until a continuous pipe discharges water.
Four types are recognised: concentrated leak through a crack, backward erosion from the exit point, suffusion of fines through coarse pores, and contact erosion along a fine–coarse interface.
Suffusion affects widely or gap-graded cohesionless soils, termed internally unstable, where fines pass between coarse grains that carry most of the effective stress.
Filters coarser and more permeable than the soil trap eroded particles but pass seepage; they must be internally stable, non-cohesive, free-draining and strong.
The critical shear stress that starts concentrated leak erosion can be estimated with the hole erosion test or the jet erosion test.

notes: Suffusion here is the same process as the Suffosion seed (soils-in-the-landscape); not drafted separately.

definition.text: A viscous downslope flow of water-saturated fine-grained material moving under gravity.

facts.text: It is a mass movement between downhill creep and mudflow: slower than a mudflow, and covered with solid material carried along by the flow.
Clay, fine sand, silt and fine pyroclastic material are prone to it; once saturated with enough water they begin to flow.
Higher water content means faster flow, so an earthflow may take minutes or years to move and can cover a few square meters or several hectares.
Draining slopes is one of the best defences; slopes undercut by rivers or construction, or made of wet clay and silt, are most at risk.

definition.text: A vegetated strip beside a stream, usually forested, that shades it and partly shields it from the effects of neighbouring land use.

facts.text: It intercepts sediment, nutrients, pesticides and other materials in surface runoff and reduces pollutants in shallow subsurface flow.
It stabilises the stream bank, so eroding banks take less farmland out of production and less silt reaches downstream lakes and reservoirs.
A typical buffer is 50 feet (15 m) wide on each side, in three zones: native grasses that first slow runoff, shrubs, and fast-growing trees that shade the water and hold the bank.
A nine-year University of Georgia study found buffers removed at least 60% of the nitrogen and at least 65% of the phosphorus from fertilizer in runoff.

definition.text: The downslope movement of waterlogged topsoil driven by seasonal freezing and thawing, closely related to solifluction.

facts.text: It is prominent in periglacial regions with snow for six to eight months a year, where spring melt releases half a year's precipitation within a couple of days.
The waterlogged topsoil flows like a liquid, so gelifluction can occur on slopes of less than half a degree.
It forms tongue-shaped lobes on slopes of 10° to 20° and terrace-like benches on gentler ones; lobes have risers of up to 5 metres (16 ft) and treads of up to 50 metres (160 ft).

definition.text: The combined mechanical and thermal erosion of ice-rich soils and sediments by an unfrozen river or stream.

facts.text: Strong flow thaws the frozen bank, and the thawed material is removed where hydraulic forces can cut into it; banks may collapse, often along ice wedges.
Melting ice inside a porous material weakens it, leaving it easy to break up and carry away.
On the Lena, spring floods break river ice up to 2 m thick, discharge rises about tenfold within days, and the banks retreat about 40 m per year.
Cold-room experiments show that water temperature, ice temperature and discharge drive thermal erosion, while high ice content in the soil slows it.

title: Soil loss tolerance

definition.text: The maximum average yearly soil loss, in tons per acre per year, that still lets a soil sustain current production economically and indefinitely; also called the T value.

facts.text: T values range from 1 to 5 tons per acre per year.
It is calculated with the formula T=υQρC+R(1−C).
Devised by the US Soil Conservation Service, it rests on the minimum rate of loss that would deplete organic matter and harm crop productivity.
In 1961–1962 US soil groups were given T values of 2 to 6 tons per acre per year, later adjusted to 1 to 5; conservation management adopted it from the mid-1960s.
In 2007, 99 million acres, 28% of US cropland, were eroding faster than T, down from 169 million acres, 40% of cropland, in 1982.
Critics note that T values vary across space, may not hold where soluble carbonates abound, as in karst, and should be weighed against actual soil loss.

contested_note: The T value's validity is questioned because it varies across space and may not apply in carbonate-rich karst regions.

title: Baer–Babinet law

definition.text: The idea that the Earth's rotation influences how rivers form, making them erode one bank more than the other.

facts.text: It holds that rivers erode mostly their right banks in the Northern Hemisphere and their left banks in the Southern Hemisphere.
Jacques Babinet proposed it in 1859 from the Coriolis force, and Karl Ernst von Baer gave a fuller explanation in 1860.
The Coriolis force is orders of magnitude weaker than local flow forces in a channel, so the effect is unlikely to matter in any one river; Einstein explained the true causes in 1926.

contested_note: The page presents it as a hypothesis whose Coriolis mechanism is too weak to matter in a given river.

definition.text: A mathematical model that simulates the flow of rivers, streams, groundwater or drainage fronts and calculates water quality.

facts.text: These models came into use in the 1960s and 1970s, when environmental laws demanded water-quality forecasts and computing power became widely available.
Physically based models represent surface runoff, subsurface flow, evapotranspiration and channel flow; stochastic models link inputs such as rainfall to outputs such as runoff statistically.
Their surface runoff element lets them assess sediment, fertilizer, pesticide and other chemical contaminants.
Robert E. Horton's work on surface runoff, joined to quantitative treatment of erosion, laid the groundwork for modern chemical transport hydrology.

definition.text: The falling of soil off banks and slopes when it loses cohesion.

facts.text: It is shallow, involving the uppermost soil layers, and has the same causes as landslides, very wet soil above all; left unchecked it can end in massive bank or slope failure.
Rising water content weakens shear strength and so cohesion; active pore water pressure can cut shear strength by up to 60%.
Bare soils slough more readily than vegetated ones because roots hold the surface, so clearing vegetation from banks and slopes raises the risk.
Loss of root strength after harvesting can lower the safety factor so far that a moderate storm brings slope failure.

definition.text: A strip of native grassland 2 to 48 meters (6.6 to 157.5 feet) wide, laid along the lowest line of a cultivated dry valley to control erosion.

facts.text: Storm runoff from cropland concentrates along the valley line, where it can cut rills and gullies that speed its transfer and worsen damage downstream.
The grass raises soil cohesion and roughness, prevents rills and gullies, slows runoff and lets it soak back in during long winter rains.
It cannot reinfiltrate runoff from heavy spring and summer storms, so earthen dams across it may be added to hold the flow back for a while.
Vegetative filter strips are different: narrower, only a few metres wide, and placed along rivers or along or within fields.

definition.text: The replanting and rebuilding of the soil of disturbed land.

facts.text: It may happen naturally through plant colonisation and succession, or be carried out to repair damage from wildfire, mining, floods or other causes.
Erosion prevention is usually the main reason: it holds soil, helps it absorb water in heavy rain and sharply reduces turbidity in nearby waters.
Early practice simply applied seed and fertilizer, usually grasses or clover, whose fibrous roots give short-term erosion control on slopes.
Mine reclamation may need soil to be amended, replaced or created, and mycorrhizal fungi are important to success, since most woody plants need them.

definition.text: The Water Erosion Prediction Project model, a physically based erosion simulation built on hydrology, plant science, hydraulics and erosion mechanics.

facts.text: An interagency team developed it to replace the Universal Soil Loss Equation; released publicly in 1995, it is widely used in the United States and elsewhere.
It takes climate, topography, soil and management inputs and returns the water balance, soil detachment and deposition along the slope, sediment delivery and vegetation growth.
It runs for single storms or continuously, on hillslopes, roads and small parcels, or on whole watersheds of linked hillslopes, channels and impoundments.
Its sediment output falls into five size classes, primary clay, silt and sand and small and large aggregates, so selective transport and enrichment of fines can be calculated.

title: National Resources Inventory

definition.text: A periodic assessment by the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service of the state of soil, water and related resources on private land.

facts.text: The survey has run at 5-year intervals since 1977, most recently in 2017, and each report compares its data with 1982.
Its summaries cover soil erosion, land use status and trends, development of non-federal rural land, and rangeland.

notes: A US federal survey with no global significance and no in-scope inlinks; kept only as the likely source of the US erosion-above-T figures (Soil loss tolerance).

definition.text: The work of restoring prairie destroyed by industrial, agricultural, commercial or residential development to its earlier state.

facts.text: Settlers plowed up the tallgrass prairie, and by 1849 most prairie grass species had given way to crops, leaving soil without the grasses' extensive fibrous roots.
Restoration helps conserve topsoil, which is exposed to wind and rain erosion once prairie is plowed under.
Prairie grasses take carbon from the air by photosynthesis and store it in the soil, making prairie soil useful for carbon sequestration.
In Europe, former cropland is restored by spontaneous succession, sowing seed mixtures, transferring plant material, and removing and transferring topsoil.

definition.text: The shear strength along a discontinuity, such as a joint, in a soil or rock mass, which strongly shapes how the mass behaves.

facts.text: It is often far lower than the strength of the intact blocks between discontinuities, and many natural and man-made slopes fail because of it.
It depends on the discontinuity's persistence, surface roughness, infill, fluid pressure, solution and cementation, and on whether it has moved before.
Weak discontinuities make deformation plastic rather than elastic, which can cause larger, permanent settlement of foundations.
Real discontinuities cannot be calculated analytically, so their strength comes from laboratory or field tests, such as the direct shear test, or from empirical characterisation.

definition.text: The use of time-domain reflectometry to watch for slope movement at highway cuts, rail beds and open-pit mines.

facts.text: A coaxial cable set in a vertical borehole with brittle grout deforms sharply when the ground moves, showing up as a peak in the reflection trace.
Once insensitive to small movements and dependent on people reading traces, it was improved by Farrington and Sargand (2004), whose numerical-derivative method gives earlier warning.
Timing infiltration with probes in different layers helps judge how well best management practices cut stormwater runoff.

definition.text: The two main ways a flow carries sediment: rolling and sliding along the bed as bed load, or held up in the water as suspended load.

facts.text: Bed load rolls, slides and hops along the bed at a small fraction of the flow speed and is usually thought to be 5–10% of a stream's total sediment load.
Suspended load moves at a large fraction of the mean flow speed; wash load, fine material from upstream, moves with the stream and is spread almost evenly through the water.
The Rouse number, set by a grain's settling velocity against turbulent upward velocity, decides its mode: above 7.5 it stays put, below 0.8 it travels as wash load.
Small particles settle more slowly than heavy ones, which governs how far downstream they travel; Stokes' law gives the settling velocity of small grains.

definition.text: A graph, drawn by Filip Hjulström in 1935, of the flow velocity needed to erode, transport or deposit sediment of each grain size.

facts.text: It uses logarithmic axes, and Åke Sundborg later added separate movement thresholds for several water depths.
It now has mainly historical value: it ignores water depth and does not show that slowing flow causes deposition and speeding flow causes erosion.
The dimensionless Shields diagram, based on shear stress, is now accepted for the start of sediment motion in rivers.

definition.text: A mode of transport in which wind or water lifts loose grains from a bed and carries them in short hops back to the surface.

facts.text: At low flow speeds grains only roll along the surface as creep; above the fluid threshold, drag and lift raise them into roughly ballistic arcs.
Landing grains splash others into motion, and in air this saltation bombardment makes most of the dust in dust storms.
Particles of about 70 micrometres or less in air are held up by turbulence and travel in suspension instead.
It moves pebbles in rivers, sand over deserts, soil blowing off fields and drifting snow; fences with holes slow it, and sand piles up on their lee side.

definition.text: A water-laden mass of soil and broken rock that flows down mountainsides, funnels into channels and leaves thick muddy deposits on valley floors.

facts.text: Its bulk density is about 2000 kilograms per cubic meter, like other landslides, yet high pore-fluid pressure liquefies the sediment so it flows almost like water.
Sediment fills more than about 40 to 50% of its volume; floods with about 10 to 40% solids are hyperconcentrated floods, and true mudflows are mostly finer than sand.
It needs slopes steeper than about 25 degrees, plenty of loose sediment, soil or weathered rock, and enough water to almost fully saturate it.
Triggers include intense rain or snowmelt, dam-break or glacial outburst floods and landslides, and debris flows become more frequent after forest and brush fires.
Flows in steep channels often exceed 10 m/s (36 km/h), and flows of up to about 100,000 cubic meters are common in mountains.
A boulder-rich head is followed by a liquefied body of finer sediment; deposits are poorly sorted lobes with boulder levees that build alluvial fans.
Debris flows killed more than 20,000 people at Armero, Colombia, in 1985 and tens of thousands in Vargas State, Venezuela, in 1999.
Debris basins can catch them, but they are a costly last resort that needs yearly maintenance.

title: Desert pavement

definition.text: A desert surface covered with closely packed, interlocking pebble- and cobble-sized rock fragments.

facts.text: A common explanation is that wind and occasional rain remove sand and dust, leaving larger stones; once formed, the pavement shields the ground from further erosion.
Fine particles collect beneath the stones as a vesicular A horizon, labelled Av.
A newer idea is that windblown dust settles between and under the stones, building soil beneath them; helium-3 dating in the Mojave Desert in 1995 found the rocks older than the soil below.
It is used as a sign of aridity and of the relative age of a surface, since older surfaces carry better-developed pavements.

contested_note: Geologists debate how desert pavements form and how old they are; deflation, clay shrink–swell and dust accretion are all proposed.

definition.text: A permeable fabric laid with soil to separate, filter, reinforce, protect or drain it.

facts.text: Geotextiles are usually polypropylene or polyester, either woven or felt-like nonwoven, and belong to the wider family of geosynthetics.
They were first meant to replace granular soil filters; in the 1950s R.J. Barrett used them behind seawalls and under erosion control blocks and riprap.
They are used in silt fences and bank protection, as matting that steadies flow in channels and swales, and to let plants grow on steep slopes.
Coir geotextiles are popular for erosion control and slope stabilization; they last about 3 to 5 years and break down into humus.

definition.text: One of four classes, A to D, into which the NRCS sorts soils by how readily they take in water, used to choose a runoff curve number.

facts.text: Group A, mostly deep well-drained sands and gravels, has a final infiltration rate above 0.30 in (7.6 mm) per hour and low runoff potential.
Group B infiltrates at 0.15–0.30 in (3.8–7.6 mm) per hour; group C, often with an impeding layer or fine texture, at 0.05–0.15 in (1.3–3.8 mm).
Group D, with high runoff potential, covers swelling clays, soils with a permanent high water table or a claypan near the surface, and shallow soils over impervious material.
The group is picked from measured infiltration rates, a soil survey such as the NRCS Web Soil Survey, or a soil professional's judgement.

definition.text: A device used in soil science and hydrology to study how soil reacts to rainfall.

facts.text: Natural rain cannot be reproduced on demand, so simulated rain speeds the study of erosion, surface runoff and leaching.
The first, in the 1930s, were sprinkling cans or pipes with holes; 1960s nozzles matched raindrop size, impact speed and evenness, and 1980s valves varied the intensity.
In the early 1990s simulators were used in the US Water Erosion Prediction Project to update the universal soil loss equation.
On bare soil, drop size and terminal velocity must be simulated accurately because they control splash erosion.

definition.text: Bodies of sediment laid down as a result of human activity since the Neolithic.

facts.text: It comes from land clearance, logging, mining, road building and urban growth, and from river engineering such as dams.
In the eastern US, soil eroded from uplands from the late 17th to the late 19th centuries buried valley floors and piled up behind low-head mill dams.
Human-caused soil erosion has raised river sediment transport by 2.3 (± 0.6) billion metric tons a year, yet reservoirs cut delivery to the coasts by 1.4 (± 0.3) billion metric tons a year.
Fine sediment can carry trace metals, nutrients, PAHs, PCBs and pesticides, and heavy metals may stay toxic in river sediment for decades to centuries.

definition.text: Treatments that steady burned slopes by offsetting fire's damage to vegetation and soil, to cut the risk of damaging runoff and erosion downhill.

facts.text: Fire burns canopy, litter, fine roots and soil organic compounds, leaving soil less protected, more water-repellent and less stable.
Heavy rain after a fire can bring catastrophic floods and debris flows; after the Thomas Fire in California, those of 2018 killed 20 people and destroyed 300 houses.
Seeding and mulching cover the soil, surfactants and flocculants counter water repellency and lost aggregation, and contour log or straw barriers shorten the slope length.
Risk peaks in the first year, so work must be quick; in the USA seeding fell from 75% of treated burned areas in the 1970s and 1980s to 30% in the 2000s.

definition.text: The rise in land elevation, usually in a river system, as sediment is deposited; also called alluviation.

facts.text: It happens where more sediment is supplied than the river can carry; the Exner equation describes the balance between sediment in transport and sediment in the bed.
Typical settings are lowland alluvial rivers, deltas and alluvial fans, which often subside slowly enough to offset the rising surface.
A drier climate can trigger it: suppressed plant growth weakens soil binding, so more sediment enters rivers just as their flow drops and they choke with sediment.
Land use, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes and faulting can also cause it; reduced aggradation was reported in 2009 to be raising flood risk in many deltas.

definition.text: Dry terrain in which soft sedimentary rocks and clay-rich soils have been deeply eroded into steep, bare ground.

facts.text: They have steep slopes, little vegetation and almost no regolith, with drainage densities of 48 to 464 kilometres of channel per square kilometre.
They form where an impermeable but easily eroded surface, sparse vegetation and rare heavy rains combine; runoff that cannot soak into the clay cuts dense networks of gullies.
The badlands of Badlands National Park erode at roughly 25 millimetres a year, and bentonite clay raises erodibility further.
Overgrazing, acid rain or acid mine drainage that strips vegetation can create anthropogenic badlands, as poor farming did at the Cheltenham Badlands in Ontario.

definition.text: The wearing away of the banks of a stream or river, as distinct from scour of its bed.

facts.text: Its two main mechanisms are fluvial erosion, the direct removal of particles by flowing water, and mass failure, when a bank's weight exceeds the soil's strength; undercutting by the first sets up the second.
Groundwater flowing out of a bank can cause seepage erosion, which when concentrated is called piping.
Vegetated banks generally erode more slowly because roots strengthen the soil, though heavy trees can load the bank top and reduce stability.
Rates are measured with erosion pins driven into the bank, repeated cross-section surveys, or aerial and satellite images compared over time.

definition.text: Mechanical erosion of the land surface by material dragged across it by running water, waves, glaciers, wind or downslope movement.

facts.text: Rock on a river or sea bed is worn away by the impact and grinding of moving particles, and the result on the rock is called abrasion.
It differs from corrosion, which is the chemical and solvent action of water on soluble rock.
Lateral corrasion widens a river by sideways erosion, while vertical corrasion deepens its valley.

definition.text: The sum of processes by which moving water, ice, wind and waves wear down the Earth's surface, lowering its elevation and relief.

facts.text: Erosion moves soil and rock from place to place, whereas denudation is the total of erosion and other processes that lower the surface.
It combines mechanical, biological and chemical weathering, erosion and mass wasting, and removes both solid particles and dissolved material.
Its rate depends on human activity, living organisms, climate, rock type, topography and tectonic activity.
Tectonic uplift, volcanoes and earthquakes expose crust to weathering and erosion; as denudation lightens the crust, it allows further uplift.
Denudation rates are usually much lower than uplift rates, and average mountain-building rates can be eight times the maximum average denudation.
Hutton and Playfair's idea that landscapes are worn down to near sea level gave rise to planation theories such as Davis's peneplanation cycle, which faded after 1964.

definition.text: The estimation of how fast a landscape is being lowered, usually expressed in centimetres or inches per 1000 years.

facts.text: The commonest method converts suspended, bed and dissolved loads at a gauging station to a volume and divides it by the watershed area upstream.
Cosmogenic isotopes, mostly 10Be and 26Al, are used because their concentration in sediment leaving a basin is inversely related to how fast the basin erodes.
Stream load can vary by up to a factor of five between successive years, and rates often assume uniform erosion.
The stream power law, E = KA^m S^n, relates erosion rate to an erodibility constant, drainage area and channel gradient.

definition.text: The geological process by which sediment, soil and rock are added to a landform or landmass.

facts.text: Wind, ice, water and gravity carry weathered material and drop it in layers when the flow loses enough kinetic energy.
Deposition starts when the forces moving sediment can no longer overcome gravity and friction, an idea known as the null point hypothesis.
Large grains in bed load or suspended load come to rest when bed shear stress and turbulence fall too low; suspended grains may travel some way as they fall through the water.
Fine silt and clay particles settle individually by Stokes' law, but in seawater they flocculate, bonding electrically into flocs.
Deposition can also build sediment from organic or chemical matter, as with chalk from plankton skeletons and coal from plant material laid down without oxygen.

definition.text: The settling of suspended particles out of a fluid until they come to rest against a barrier.

facts.text: Settling is the fall of particles through the liquid; sedimentation is its end result.
Type 1 particles such as sand settle singly at constant velocity, type 2 particles flocculate so their settling velocity changes, and above 1000 mg/L type 3 particles settle together as a zone.
Geological rates range from under 3 millimetres per thousand years for deep-sea sediment to several metres per thousand years in parts of major deltas.
Sedimentation-enhancing strategies restore water and sediment exchange between rivers and delta plains so that subsiding deltas can keep their elevation.

definition.text: The incorporation of surface sediment into a moving fluid such as air, water or ice, as part of erosion.

facts.text: Each grain size has a flow velocity, the entrainment velocity, at which grains begin to move.
Once moving, grains keep travelling below that velocity because friction with the bed is reduced, and settle only when the flow slows further, as the Hjulström curve shows.

title: Fluvial sediment processes

definition.text: The movement of sediment by rivers and streams, with the erosion, deposition and landforms it creates.

facts.text: Flowing water exerts shear stress on the bed and lowers it where the bed is weak or loose; carried sediment abrades the bed while the fragments themselves are worn smaller and rounder by attrition.
Sediment travels as bed load, suspended load or dissolved material.
Where flow is fast more particles are picked up than dropped, and where it is slow the dropped particles build floodplains of alluvium.
The Rouse number, settling velocity over upward velocity, sets a grain's mode: above 2.5 bed load, 0.8 to 2.5 suspended load, below 0.8 wash load.
Water moves larger sediment than air because it is denser and more viscous; floods can carry cobbles and boulders.
The Mississippi is estimated to carry 406 million tons of sediment to the sea each year, the Yellow River 796 million tons and the Po 67 million tons.
Sediment motion builds ripples, dunes and antidunes, which preserved in rock record the direction and strength of past flows.

notes: The Yellow River load here (796 million tons, S:01683427e390) differs from the 1.6 billion tons in 'Sediment pollution of waterways'; the sources do not say they measure the same quantity or period.

definition.text: Erosion at the head of a stream channel that moves its origin upslope, lengthening the stream, valley or gully and enlarging its drainage basin.

facts.text: Once a stream starts cutting back, the steep gradient at its head speeds the erosion.
Water collecting in channels gains speed and erosive power, cutting into and extending the heads of gullies.
Given time, a stream can break into a neighbouring watershed and capture its drainage, as the Shenandoah River did to Potomac tributaries.
It produces dendritic patterns on uniform bedrock, trellis patterns on alternating weak and strong rock, and rectangular patterns on jointed rock.

definition.text: The distinction between the conditions that make a slope vulnerable to failure (causes) and the single event that finally sets it moving (trigger).

facts.text: A landslide can have many causes but only one trigger, which is usually easy to identify afterwards but hard to predict beforehand.
Causes are grouped as geological (weathered or jointed material), morphological (slope angle, erosion, vegetation change), physical and human (deforestation, excavation, mining).
Following Terzaghi, internal causes weaken the material's resistance to shear stress, while external causes increase the shear stress.
Earthquakes trigger slides by shaking and by raising pore water pressure; topographic amplification makes ground accelerations strongest at slope crests.

definition.text: Landslides set off by heavy or prolonged rain, the main trigger in most cases.

facts.text: Of 210 damaging landslide events worldwide in the year to September 2003, over 90% were triggered by heavy rainfall.
Rain raises pore water pressure, which buoys the slope material and reduces its resistance to movement; groundwater flow can add a downslope push.
Water can also destabilise slopes by fluidising old debris into debris flows, removing suction in silty soils, undercutting the toe and causing soil piping.
Caine's 1980 worldwide threshold, I = 14.82 D^-0.39 (intensity in mm per hour, duration in hours), applies over 10 minutes to 10 days.

title: Mineral dust

definition.text: An atmospheric aerosol of suspended soil minerals, mainly oxides and carbonates.

facts.text: It is mostly the crustal oxides SiO2, Al2O3, FeO, Fe2O3 and CaO and the carbonates CaCO3 and MgCO3.
Global emissions are estimated at 1000 to 5000 million tons a year, mostly from deserts; about a quarter may come from human desertification and land-use change.
The Sahara is the largest source, at 60 to 200 million tons a year, and its dust feeds nutrients to the Amazon rainforest and Mediterranean phytoplankton.
Spring dust from the Gobi, called Asian dust, harms visibility and health but is thought to enrich soils with trace minerals; farming pressure and desertification worsened it after 1950.
Soil moisture, vegetation cover, wind speed and soil type control dust emissions.
North American dust deposition has risen sharply since the early 1800s, with a 60% increase in the 1800s from accelerating land disturbance.
Modern observations link drought to more dust, but lake-sediment records of megadroughts show both increases and no change in deposition.

contested_note: Modern observations tie drought to higher dust levels, while paleo records of megadroughts disagree on whether deposition rose.

definition.text: A shear stress rewritten in units of velocity, also called friction velocity.

facts.text: It is used to describe dispersion of particles and contaminants, the velocity profile near a flow's boundary, and sediment transport in channels.
It scales well with bedload transport, and in most rivers it is between 5% and 10% of the mean flow velocity.
Near the ground, the log wind profile lets friction velocity be found from wind speeds measured at two heights.
The zero-plane displacement, where wind speed falls to zero among trees or buildings, is roughly 2/3 to 3/4 of obstacle height.

definition.text: A dimensionless number used to calculate when sediment begins to move in a fluid flow.

facts.text: Developed by Albert F. Shields, it is a non-dimensional shear stress, θ = τ / ((ρs − ρ) g D), with τ the shear stress, ρs and ρ the sediment and fluid densities and D the grain diameter.
It is proportional to the ratio of the fluid force on a particle to the particle's weight.
The critical Shields number marks the onset of motion; shear stress belongs to the current, critical shear stress to the sediment.
The Shields diagram, using critical shear stress and Reynolds number, is considered more precise than the Hjulström curve for estimating suspended load.

definition.text: Water pollution by fine silt and clay particles, both as raised suspended sediment and as unwanted fine deposits on the bottom.

facts.text: It is most often caused by soil erosion or by sediment spilled during dredging and dumping.
In rural areas the source is usually soil degraded by intensive or poor farming, especially fine-grained soils such as loess; in towns it is construction sites stripped of vegetation.
Because erosion at the source may be a fraction of a millimetre a year, sediment is measured in transport: concentration times discharge, so 50 mg/L at 30 m3/s gives 1.5 kg/s.
Suspended sediment disrupts filter-feeding organisms and deposits bury them; as little as 1 mm of accumulation may kill coral polyps.
Hard-bottom communities and mussel and oyster banks are more sensitive than sand and mud bottoms.
The first defence is keeping land covered to prevent erosion, the second is trapping sediment before it reaches streams; construction sites use short exposure times and silt screens.
Silt also fills navigation and irrigation channels, where dredging is often the only remedy once it has settled.

definition.text: The energy that flowing water in a river or stream expends on its bed and banks, first derived by R. A. Bagnold in the 1960s.

facts.text: It is the product of water density, gravitational acceleration, discharge and slope: Ω = ρgQS, in watts per unit length of channel.
Unit stream power divides by channel width, allowing rivers of different widths to be compared and giving a better estimate of sediment carrying capacity.
Critical unit stream power is the power needed to move a grain of given size, and it sets a river's competence, the largest grain it can move.
Several studies found that rivers shift from stable to actively reshaping themselves at a unit stream power of 30 to 35 W m−2.
It is used widely in landscape evolution and river incision models, and to design bridges and culverts that avoid starting erosion.

definition.text: The part of a flow's sediment that is lifted off the bed and held up in the fluid by turbulence.

facts.text: It is mostly fine sand, silt and clay, though stronger flows carry coarser sand low in the water column.
It forms the middle layer of fluvial transport, between bed load below and the finest wash load above, and a particle can shift between them as flow speed changes.
Grains are fully suspended at Rouse numbers of 0.8 to 1.2 and half suspended at 1.2 to 2.5; above 2.5 they move as bed load.
Suspended load needs flow velocity to stay up and is deposited when the flow slows.

definition.text: A model that estimates a field's potential average annual soil loss to wind, used to design wind erosion control.

facts.text: It is written E = f(I, K, C, L, V): soil erodibility, ridge roughness, a climatic factor, the unsheltered distance across the field and the equivalent vegetative cover.
Soil starts moving above a critical wind speed, and the erosion rate follows the cube of the friction velocity.
Friction velocity is calculated from wind speed at a measured height using the von Kármán constant, about 0.4, in line with the logarithmic wind profile.
Wind records mostly come from airports and military bases, often only since the Second World War, which limits erosion research.

definition.text: A free, open-source hydrology model and GIS simulation sponsored by the USDA, known as SWAT.

facts.text: It is a well-known geographic hydrological model used by many universities and government agencies worldwide, and it works with commercial GIS products such as ArcGIS.

definition.text: The progressive internal erosion of soil by seeping water, which carves subsurface pipes that discharge water downstream.

facts.text: Badlands sometimes contain well-developed piping, a subsurface system of pipes, joints and caverns through which water drains.
Concentrated seepage out of a stream bank erodes a pipe of soil, and collapsing pipes in dispersive soils help form gullies.
Piping can destabilise loose earth on slopes during rain, and in earthen dams a small leak can enlarge into a channel that leads to failure.

definition.text: A strip of grass or other permanent vegetation that shields riparian areas from runoff carrying sediment, pesticides, pathogens and nutrients.

facts.text: Filter strips along field edges intercept runoff material before it leaves the field.
They work best when other conservation practices steer water towards them, and once mainly agricultural they are now common in towns.
They should not be confused with grassed waterways.
The GIS tool AgBufferBuilder designs filter strips around fields using terrain analysis of uneven runoff.

definition.text: A revised form of the Universal Soil Loss Equation, known as RUSLE, still used to estimate soil erosion.

facts.text: RUSLE and the WEPP model are two of the most widely used soil erosion models in North America.
Various techniques have emerged to compute its five factors.
Its support practice (P) factor is often estimated from land use and slope gradient, lower values meaning better erosion control.
Much of the literature on erosion of mined land focuses on fitting or improving RUSLE parameters.

definition.text: The quantity of sediment per unit area of a watershed that a river removes over a period of time.

facts.text: Monitoring it shows ecologists the health of river ecosystems, the rate of erosion and the effects of human activity.
Switching from grains to potatoes in late 19th-century Poland raised sediment yields so much that meandering rivers became braided.
Dams, reservoirs and sediment detention basins upstream reduce it.
WEPP watershed runs link hillslopes, channels and impoundments to predict sediment yield from a whole catchment.
